name: Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng National Park
blurb: Limestone forest above the caves: Hatinh langurs, bats and Annamite wildlife.

tip.title: Clear the lowland forest
tip.text: Lowland trees such as Hopea feed the langurs, doucs, muntjac and serow. Set Hopea to -100% and watch the leaf-eaters, then the bear that hunts them.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng National Park
Wikipedia: Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng National Park

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng National Park, Hatinh langur, Saola). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.name: Butterflies and moths
nodes.desc: The park has recorded 259 butterfly species. Caterpillars eat leaves and the adults are food for birds, bats and ants.
Wikipedia confirms the bear in the park. It is mostly a plant eater but also eats insects, grubs and carrion and kills hoofed animals such as muntjac and serow.
Heavy seasonal rain keeps the wet evergreen forest growing and feeds the underground rivers of the karst.
Light reaching the forest canopy and understory drives plant growth in the tropical forest.

nodes.name: Soil fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, dead wood and bat droppings, returning nutrients to the thin karst soil.

link_ideas.what: The park borders the Hin Namno karst area in Laos, so forest animals can range across the border.

story: Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng National Park in central Vietnam protects one of the world's two largest karst regions, with 300 caves and grottoes. A 2009 survey put the discovered cave length at about 126 km. The park borders Hin Namno National Park in Laos.
matters: Sơn Đoòng Cave was found in that 2009 survey. The limestone forest shelters the threatened Hatinh langur, found primarily in Quảng Bình Province.
